archetype.name: Bubble Team (possession upgrade)
archetype.definition: A club whose 5-on-5 play looks like a playoff team's after a 25th-place season, but which hasn't yet turned that territorial edge into a separating record because the power play and the backup goalie keep handing points back.

report.headline: The Blues are driving play now; the record just hasn't caught up yet.
report.take:
Six games in, St. Louis is 3-2-1 and sits fifth in a crowded Central. That record is the least interesting thing about them. The Blues own 55.1% of the 5-on-5 expected goals, 7th in the league, and 53% of the shot attempts, 10th. Last season they finished 25th on this site with a 49.3% expected-goals share and a negative goal differential. A team that spent last year getting out-chanced is now the one tilting the ice. Their PDO of 99.8 is dead average, so this is not a hot-shooting mirage.

The offense is the engine, and it runs deeper than one line. Mason McTavish has driven it: 7 points, 23 shots and a 66.7% xGF share, good for 8th of 213 on the centers tab. Behind him, Connor McMichael, Pavel Buchnevich, Jimmy Snuggerud, Pius Suter and Jake Neighbours have all chipped in, and the listed forwards have 17 goals between them. That has produced the 8th-ranked offense. The blueline adds puck movement but almost no finishing, with one goal from the whole group. The penalty kill has gone from a liability last season (76.7%) to a strength (89.5%, 7th).

The numbers hide a two-goalie story. Joel Hofer has been excellent: .921, a shutout, +2.5 GSAx and 7th of 64 on the goalies tab. Jordan Binnington's two starts produced an .847 save percentage and -3.6 GSAx, which is enough to drag the team figure into the red (-1.6, 22nd). The other drags are a 14.3% power play (25th) and a top center, Robert Thomas, with 2 points and no goals despite 19-plus minutes a night and a 57.2% xGF share. That is a slump profile, not a decline profile. The defense also leaks to opposing centers: 54% of the points it allows go to them, against a league norm of 37.5%.

Where is this heading? The process numbers say a team that should rise above its .500-ish record, not regress toward last year. Last season's 37-33-12 was propped up by close-game luck (+2.8 points over the goal differential). This year's points are slightly below what the margin implies. If the power play climbs toward average and the crease tilts toward Hofer, this is a playoff-caliber profile. Six games is a thin sample, though, and the step up has to survive the Central's better teams.

strengths.title: Tilting the ice at 5-on-5
strengths.body: St. Louis has the 7th-best expected-goals share and a top-10 shot-attempt share, a sharp turn from last year's sub-50% xGF. Most of the regular forwards are above 50% in their own xGF splits, so it isn't one line carrying the numbers. With PDO at 99.8, nothing about this is propped up by luck. Possession edges are among the stickier early-season signals, but six games are still six games.

strengths.title: McTavish leads a deep attack
strengths.body: McTavish is producing like a top-10 center, and his shot volume suggests the scoring is earned rather than lucky. Behind him, scoring is spread across most of the top nine, which is why the offense ranks 8th even with the top-minute center and the power play both cold. McTavish's finishing will probably cool. A Thomas rebound should offset it.

strengths.title: Hofer and a rebuilt penalty kill
strengths.body: Hofer has been one of the league's better goalies so far, saving goals above expected with a shutout already. The penalty kill has jumped from last season's 76.7% to 89.5%. Some of that kill rate will drift down, since a sub-80% team doesn't usually become elite overnight. Hofer's form matters more, because he decides how much of the territorial edge survives.

concerns.title: Binnington's starts sink the team
concerns.body: Two starts at .847 and -3.6 GSAx have pushed the team GSAx down to 22nd despite Hofer's strong work. It's a tiny sample, but last season's team GSAx was also deep in the negatives, so goaltending is not a solved problem. How the starts get split from here is the biggest lever on the record.

concerns.title: A power play that isn't working
concerns.body: At 14.3%, the power play ranks 25th. That wastes the even-strength edge, and it was only middling last season too. With this many skilled forwards, some improvement is likely. This week brings two top-four penalty kills, though, so it may not come soon.

concerns.title: Opposing centers feast; Thomas is quiet
concerns.body: The defense ranks 28th at holding centers under their expected output, and centers take a far larger share of the points against than the league norm. At the other end, Thomas has 2 points and no goals in heavy minutes, even though his on-ice chance share is healthy. His slump should break. The middle-of-the-ice leak is a structural issue worth watching against Minnesota and Winnipeg.

trend.note: A 4-0 opening win gave way to a three-game skid that included a 1-6 loss in Colorado. The Blues have since won two straight, scoring 12 goals in those games while their underlying shares stayed strong throughout.

weekAhead.headline: A stiff test in Minnesota, then two winnable games
weekAhead.body:
The road trip opens against the toughest opponent of the three. Minnesota is 6th on the site, with the 4th-best defense by goals against, an A- goaltending grade with +4.7 GSAx, and the league's best power play at 36.8%. The Wild don't out-chance teams, though: their xGF share is 49.7%, 20th. That makes it a test of whether St. Louis can turn possession into goals against a hot goalie. The Blues' penalty discipline matters more than usual here.

Nashville is the softest stop. The Predators are 24th on the site, with D grades at forward and on the blueline, and they rank 27th in xGF share and 29th in shot attempts. They also give up a lot to centers, which sets up well for McTavish and Thomas. Winnipeg comes to St. Louis at 4-1-1, but the Jets lead the league in points above their goal differential and sit 26th in xGF share. Their record outruns their play much as the Blues' play outruns their record. Winnipeg does have a top-three penalty kill and holds centers in check, so the Blues likely need to win that game at even strength.

keyMatchups.title: Blues' discipline vs. Wild power play
keyMatchups.body: Minnesota converts 36.8% of its power plays, and St. Louis's improved kill will be tested. The Blues should control 5-on-5 play, but penalties would hand the game to the Wild's strength. Minnesota's goalies are also saving well above expected, so even-strength goals may be scarce.

keyMatchups.title: Blues centers vs. Nashville's middle
keyMatchups.body: Nashville is out-chanced badly and ranks 26th at holding centers below expectation. That's an opening for McTavish and a chance for Thomas to break his goalless start. This is the game St. Louis should dominate on the shot clock.

keyMatchups.title: Possession vs. Winnipeg's close-game luck
keyMatchups.body: The Jets have the most points above their goal differential in the league, yet they're out-chanced at 5-on-5. Their B+ goaltending and stingy defense against centers will make the Blues work for it. Over a full season, the Blues' chance edge should beat Winnipeg's close-game luck. In one game, the goaltending matchup may decide it.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal. Hofer in two of three games makes a winning week likely, while another rough Binnington start could undo the possession edge.

restOfSeason.body:
The underlying shift looks real. Expected-goals and shot-attempt shares this strong, paired with an average PDO, usually lead to more wins, not fewer. Last year's team overachieved its margin, while this one is slightly underachieving it. Expect the 89.5% penalty kill to drift back toward the pack and McTavish's pace to cool. Expect the power play to improve from 25th and Thomas to start producing at a top-line rate. The net effect should be a team scoring above league average while allowing about an average number of goals.

The swing is in net. If Hofer takes the bulk of the starts and stays near his current level, St. Louis has the profile of a playoff team in the Central. If the starts stay split and Binnington doesn't recover, the Blues stay on the bubble no matter how they control play. The 2-3-1 start for Dallas and the strong early records of Utah and Winnipeg say the division order is still fluid.
swingFactors: Hofer vs. Binnington split in goal
Power play climbing toward league average

confidence.note: Six games. The possession numbers are encouraging, but goalie and special-teams rates are very noisy at this sample.
